1.pericope_label: The heading: a written record of the marches

schools.summary: Gill offers both constructions of the disputed clause — either the journeys were made at God's commandment, which is how Aben Ezra joins the words and how the narrative elsewhere states it, since Israel halted while the cloud rested and moved when it rose; or Moses wrote the account at God's commandment, so that it might stand on record for later ages and prove that Israel really had been led about a wilderness whose places bore no names but the ones they gave them. Calvin asks why so full a list appears now, when earlier narrative gave only the memorable halts, and answers from three purposes: local description lends certainty to history, the names recall how often the nation provoked God, and standing on Canaan's threshold they were to recognise that their own stubbornness had sent them wandering by tortuous routes — while recognising too that God preserved the despisers of his grace and carried the covenant forward to their children.

Henry is interested in how the register came to be written. God ordered Moses at the outset to keep a journal, entering the remarkable occurrences of the way, so that reviewing it might satisfy him and publishing it might instruct others — from which Henry advises private Christians, and men in public station especially, to preserve some written account of God's providences toward them, since our memories are treacherous and want the help.

Clarke treats the chapter as a document: the book may fairly be called a diary and indeed the first book of travels ever published, and enough evidence survives that many stages can be identified from descriptions particular enough to fix them, though by no means all. He allows a broad typology — Israel as the church in the wilderness, its unsettled wandering answering to religion under the law and the entry under Joshua to the fixed salvation provided by Christ — but refuses to press it further. Wesley repeats Henry's counsel about keeping a record almost word for word.

Keil and Delitzsch insist the opening noun denotes not a station but the striking of a camp, and so a train or march, which is why the itinerary describes Israel's progress by the places they left rather than those they occupied and repeats throughout that they broke up. Ellicott takes the word the same way, adds that the encampments lasted very unequal periods and may have averaged a twelvemonth apiece, and balances the record's two faces — a memorial of the nation's sin and rebellion on one side, of God's faithfulness and long-suffering on the other.

debates: What 'by the commandment of the Lord' governs. Gill sets out both readings — that the journeys were undertaken at God's command, as Aben Ezra joins the words, or that Moses wrote the register at his command — and Ellicott states the alternative without deciding between them.
outliers: Ainsworth took the forty-two stations to signify the forty-two generations from Abraham to Christ, and Bromley read each name and place as describing a spiritual state through which the soul passes on its way to the kingdom. Clarke reports both and dismisses them: in cases of this kind, he says, fancy has much more to do than judgment.

3.pericope_label: From Rameses, with a high hand

schools.summary: Gill takes Rameses for the city in which Israel was gathered into one body shortly before departure, and reports the Targum of Jonathan's Pelusium and Dr Shaw's guess at Cairo; on the burial of the firstborn he notes the practical effect — hearts heavy, hands full, other work in front of them — and that the Egyptians knew why the blow had fallen. Calvin rejects the view that the name stands for the whole land of Goshen, since a simultaneous start from scattered places is unreasonable and fits ill with their going forth in orderly array, and supposes instead a muster in the neighbourhood so that the column might be organised. He reads the Egyptians as witnesses of their own defeat, so subdued they dared not lift a finger, and is careful that they refrained from obstruction not for want of leisure but because God's power had drained away their capacity to resist.

Clarke calls Rameses the metropolis of Goshen and the rendezvous of the whole nation, likewise supposing it Cairo. Wesley reads the judgment on Egypt's gods concretely and doubly: the false gods were the beasts those worshippers adored, and these died when the firstborn of man and beast were struck, while their images too were probably thrown down, as Dagon afterwards fell before the ark.

debates: Whether Egypt's idols literally fell. Wesley thinks the images were probably thrown down, as Dagon was before the ark; Calvin calls it a silly notion that every idol toppled of its own accord, holding that the clause means God triumphed over them by proving they could not help their worshippers and by exposing the magicians' trickery.
themes: judgment on the gods of Egypt

5.pericope_label: Succoth to the wilderness of Sinai

schools.summary: Gill measures the stages in miles and supplies what history attaches to them — that the halt by the sea goes unmentioned in Exodus, that the departure from the wilderness of Sin followed the manna, that the Targum of Jonathan renders Alush the strong fort where Israel first kept a sabbath, and that Sinai gave the decalogue with every statute and the directions for the tabernacle. On the turning toward Pihahiroth he follows Aben Ezra in referring it to cloud and people together, and denies that Israel had been there before and doubled back. Calvin reads the same stages for what they cost and proved: the three days' march celebrates God's power rather than the people's endurance, since no water was found between the sea and Marah, and their rebellion over a bitter taste was the more detestable for it — while the twelve springs and seventy palms of Elim show God's mercy to churlish men. From what Moses passes over in silence Calvin infers the chapter's whole purpose, to set the forty years' wandering before the nation's eyes.

Clarke numbers the stations and asks what each name attaches to. Succoth means booths and probably denotes no settlement at all; Etham, Dophkah and Alush he gives up as unknown; Marah he places at Sedur on Shaw's authority; at Elim, Shaw counted only nine of the twelve wells but upwards of two thousand palms in place of seventy. The encampment by the sea he finds hardest, since Israel was by then bearing east and moving further from the water, and he supposes the name taken from having the sea still in view. He also protests the name Red Sea itself: nothing about that water or its sand is red, the Hebrew means the weedy sea, and the Greek version turned it red with the Latin and the European translations following — in opposition, he says, to etymology and reason alike.

themes: no water between the sea and Marah

schools.summary: Gill explains the first name from its story — the people lusted after flesh and murmured, the flesh came and a pestilence with it, and those who died were buried on the spot, whence a name meaning the graves of lust — remembers Hazeroth as where Miriam was struck with leprosy, and gives Rithmah the fullest treatment: the Targum of Jonathan glossing the name from the juniper that grew there, travellers finding the valley still called Ritma with two cisterns of excellent water, and some learned men making it Kadesh-barnea itself, with Jarchi finding the name apt for the evil tongue of the spies. Through the unidentifiable stretch that follows he simply keeps counting miles.

Clarke insists Kibroth-hattaavah was no city or village but bare desert named from the plague, reports Shaw's computation of Hazeroth at some thirty miles from Sinai, and supposes Rithmah named from the abundance of juniper somewhere in the wilderness of Paran. For the rest he records ignorance without embroidery: Libnah uncertain, Rissah nowhere else in Scripture and its site utterly uncertain, Kehelathah utterly unknown and unlikely to be Keilah, mount Shapher undeterminable, Haradah unknown though Calmet suggested the Bered of Genesis, and Makheloth found nowhere else at all.

debates: Why Taberah is missing from the list. Gill offers two answers — either it was the same place as Kibroth-hattaavah or lay close beside it, or, on Aben Ezra's view, Israel camped there a single day and so it does not rank among the journeys; Clarke reasons instead from the three days' march needed to reach this point, inferring that other unremarkable stations stood between and went unrecorded.

28.pericope_label: Mithcah to Mount Hor; the death of Aaron

schools.summary: Gill goes on counting where Clarke goes on identifying, his figures lengthening as the wandering does, and supplies the arithmetic of Aaron's hundred and twenty-three years — eighty-three when he stood before Pharaoh, forty since spent with Israel, and three years the elder of Moses. Calvin asks why the age is stated at all and makes it part of the argument: at a hundred Aaron had already outrun the ordinary span, yet an extraordinary blessing kept him alive until the nation stood on the edge of its inheritance, so that Israel's failure to acknowledge that fatherly care was the baser for it. On king Arad he notes that Moses gives no account of the fighting and merely revives the recollection, the point being that Israel now met an enemy for the first time and began to engage one of the nations of Canaan — the opening of their warfare, at the moment the promised inheritance was about to be entered.

Clarke leaves Mithcah to Calmet's conjecture of Mocha in Arabia Petraea, notes that some take Hashmonah for Azmon, reads Hor-hagidgad as the pit of Gidgad and supposes some vast cavern gave it the name, and gives up Jotbathah, Ebronah and Bene-jaakan. Two stations he can fix: Ezion-gaber, which Shaw put on the western shore of the Elanitic gulf some sixty miles from Sinai and which the Arabs still call the golden port because Solomon's ships sailed thence for Ophir; and Zin, which is Kadesh, remembered for Miriam's death and the water from the rock, and from which Israel had to bear right toward Mount Hor because Edom refused them passage.
Keil and Delitzsch decline to treat the remaining names here at all, referring each of them back to the narrative chapters in which the events belonging to them were recorded.

debates: Where Aaron died, and in what order Moseroth and Bene-jaakan were reached. Deuteronomy has Israel arriving at Mosera from Bene-jaakan and places Aaron's death there, whereas this chapter reverses the order and puts the death at Hor. Gill follows Jarchi in supposing they doubled back, Hashmonah to Moserah to Bene-jaakan and to Moserah again; Clarke resolves it geographically instead, making Mosera, Moseroth and Hor three names for one site, or Moseroth a village standing near the mountain.

41.pericope_label: Zalmonah to the plains of Moab

schools.summary: Gill accounts for the missing stations by supposing the removes the earlier narrative records between Almon-diblathaim and Beer were short shifts of camp rather than stations properly so called, explains Dibon-gad from Gad's later rebuilding of it in the valley of Zared, measures the last removes at sixteen miles apiece, derives Abarim from the nearby Jordan crossings, and fixes the final camp by Eusebius at ten miles from Jericho on the far bank. He also reports the common Jewish estimate, which the Jerusalem Targum states as a question and answer, that the camp stretched twelve miles from Beth-jesimoth to Abel-shittim, and explains the prefix of that name as mourning, commemorating the plague in which twenty-four thousand died.

Clarke reads the first names etymologically — Zalmonah from the word for an image, guessing the brazen serpent gave it the name, and remarking that the term corrupted into talisman comes from the same root; Ije-abarim as heaps or protuberances, so probably low mounds near a Jordan ford. He notes that Almon-diblathaim was Moabite territory in Jeremiah's day, that the mountains of Abarim are where Moses died, that the plains of Moab were the scene of everything between Balaam and Balak, and that Beth-jesimoth afterwards fell to the Reubenites. Wesley gives the same account of Abel-shittim as mourning and attaches it to the sin in the matter of Peor.

Ellicott devotes his longest note in the chapter to reconciling this list with the earlier one, which gives seven intermediate stations where this gives three, none of them sharing a name. On the count he proposes that the earlier chapter records only stations of historical importance while this records every place where an organised camp was pitched and the tent of meeting formally raised; on the names he appeals to scale, since six hundred thousand men with their families and cattle could have occupied several towns at once, as this chapter itself shows in stretching the camp from Beth-jesimoth to Abel-shittim. Of the last station he has no doubt at all, since Nebo was a peak of Pisgah and Pisgah one of the mountains of Abarim.

50.pericope_label: Drive out the inhabitants, destroy the idols

schools.summary: Gill supplies the setting and the audience, the word coming in the plains of Moab by Jordan near Jericho and concerning the whole body of the people. Calvin insists the two halves of the command belong together: he has explained elsewhere why God willed these nations expelled — lest they adulterate his pure worship, corrupt Israel by example, and stand as pollutions in a holy land — but here Moses is making a different point, beginning his account of the division by saying the country must first be emptied so that its free and full enjoyment might remain for Israel. Since the clauses run on together, dispossess and dwell and for I have given you the land, Calvin thinks it absurd to detach one from the other, the gift being what makes the dispossession intelligible.

Henry reads the command against the forty years before it and finds a purpose in the wandering itself: total separation from every other people kept Israel clear of the temptation to idolatry, so that the idols of Egypt might be forgotten and the generation entering Canaan be men who had never known those depths of Satan. Crossing Jordan meant walking back into that temptation. Nothing whatever was to be preserved — not as monuments of antiquity to gratify the curious, not as ornaments for houses, not as toys for children — partly as declared abhorrence of idolatry and partly to remove the temptation. He states the consequences as maxims: learn not their way and then fear not their power; spare either the idols or the idolaters and you foster snakes in your own bosom; if we do not drive sin out, sin will drive us out.

Keil and Delitzsch treat the closing verses as one command in two halves — exterminate the Canaanites, and divide their land among Israel's families — and note that a single Hebrew verb carries both movements, to take possession of and so to drive others out of possession.

52.pericope_label: The images broken; the land divided by lot

schools.summary: Gill reads the expulsion as an aim rather than an event, accomplished gradually with Israel using their utmost endeavours, and keeps the plain sense of the dispossession — turn them out of their cities, towns and houses, and live in them. Calvin asks why a lottery and answers first from human nature, since no tribe would have submitted to being sent here or there at another man's option and the judges' votes would have produced quarrels rather than settlements. But the deeper reason is that God thereby proved Israel held the land by his liberality: the lot is governed by God though men reckon nothing more fortuitous, and it fell out exactly as Jacob had prophesied — Zebulun by the sea, Asher with the fat bread and royal dainties, Judah rich in vines and pasture. What might have looked ridiculous in a dying exile parcelling out a country he did not own, God sealed at last.

Clarke derives the word rendered pictures from a root meaning to resemble and thinks it covers pictures, carved work or embroidery so far as these displayed the abominations of idolatry, while the molten images he takes for metallic talismanic figures cast under particular constellations and credited with extraordinary virtues. Wesley is blunter about the people — driving out means not banishing but destroying — and defines the furniture as stones curiously engraven and set up for worship, and chapels, altars and groves erected on the high places.

Ellicott renders the disputed word imagery or engraved figures, notes that where Leviticus names the material it is stone shaped into an idol, and refers the high places to the altars built on them. Keil and Delitzsch divide the terms by material — a stone idol, images cast from brass, and bamoth — and observe that the command to divide by lot repeats an earlier one verbatim, giving the idiom literally: whatever the lot coming out of the urn points to shall be that family's portion.

outliers: Some read the casting of lots as a figure of how we obtain a heavenly inheritance by God's gratuitous good pleasure. Calvin answers that the facts will not carry it: Hebron belonged to the inheritance yet Caleb received it without any lot, and Reuben, Gad and half Manasseh took the territory beyond Jordan by the consent of the rest rather than by lot at all — so readers should abstain from such conceits, lest they confess with shame that they have caught at an empty shadow.

55.pericope_label: Pricks in your eyes and thorns in your sides

schools.summary: Gill defines the failure before the punishment — being remiss and careless, declining the proper means, or worse, striking covenants, intermarrying and suffering them to remain — and spells out the mechanism of the sentence: mingling with the Canaanites, learning their works and serving their gods, Israel would be delivered into enemy hands and carried captive into other lands. Calvin weighs the guilt on both sides. Canaan's destruction was the just reward of four hundred years of abused forbearance, since gross indulgence of sin had begun there as far back as Abraham's day; yet Israel deserved the threatened punishment twice over, failing in the duty of executing God's vengeance, contenting themselves with part of a land wholly given them, and wilfully entangling themselves with nations God had separated them from. That the sentence took effect he proves from Judges, and observes the infliction was still running as late as David's reign.

Clarke works the metaphor itself: nothing is more vexatious than a continual goading on both sides, so that escaping the one throws the body harder against the other, and nothing more distressing than a perpetual pricking in the eye, which harasses the mind, torments the body and puts out the sight. He notes that pious men have long taken the surviving Canaanites for an emblem of indwelling sin, and follows the comparison to its bitter end — while conscience stays tender such a man feels straitened in all his goings, but being fatally persuaded that sin must dwell in him as long as he lives he adjusts his mind to the situation, his conscience loses its tenderness, and he settles for expecting redemption where and when it was never promised, beyond the grave.

Ellicott would render the last verse as a comparison rather than a sequel — as I have determined to do unto them, so will I do unto you — and observes what the history bears out, that the idolaters of Canaan were never wholly exterminated, that their pernicious influence was felt through the whole of Israel's story, and that the threatened judgments were executed at last in the Assyrian and Babylonian captivities.
